scenario_stem:
Calderwell Creamery Ltd is a private limited company in Country X that pasteurises milk and makes cheese for regional supermarkets. For the year ended 31 March 2026, the income statement showed Revenue of $540,000, Cost of Sales of $324,000, Gross Profit of $216,000, Expenses of $132,000 and Profit for the year of $84,000. A dividend of $30,000 was paid to shareholders, leaving a Retained Profit of $54,000.

The directors must decide between Option 1, a special dividend of $20,000 for loyal shareholders, and Option 2, investing $50,000 in a new pasteuriser to raise production capacity. Current assets are $180,000 and current liabilities are $72,000, giving working capital of $108,000. The gross profit margin was 40% this year, up on 37% last year.

questions.model_answer: Gross Profit is the profit made after deducting the cost of producing or buying the goods sold, calculated as Revenue minus Cost of Sales, before deducting Expenses [2].

Calculated before any expenses are deducted

Reason 2: Profit rewards shareholders for their investment [k], which allowed the $30,000 dividend to be paid and supports investor confidence in the company [app].

Point 2: It shows Retained Profit of $54,000 after the $30,000 dividend [k], so the $50,000 pasteuriser is feasible from internal funds with $4,000 headroom [app], leaving directors free to reject new debt for this purchase [an].

After a dividend of $48,000, Retained Profit was $72,000.

Option 2 is investing $40,000 in a liquid-ice machine to cut trout spoilage. The directors want a decision this month.

Directors are weighing Option 1, raising prices by 5% which should add about $19,000 of Revenue a year if volumes hold, against Option 2, cutting Expenses by $9,000 a year through energy-efficient saws and LED workshop lighting. In the year ended 31 July 2026, Revenue rose to $410,000, Cost of Sales to $287,000, Gross Profit to $123,000 and Profit for the year fell to $25,000 after Expenses of $98,000.

scenario_stem:
Fernglen Enamelware Ltd is a private limited company in Country X pressing and enamelling steel kitchenware, sold in department stores and by mail order. For the year ended 30 November 2026, the income statement showed Revenue of $520,000, Cost of Sales of $312,000, Gross Profit of $208,000, Expenses of $140,000 and Profit for the year of $68,000. A dividend of $28,000 left Retained Profit of $40,000.

A supermarket chain has offered an own-brand contract worth $200,000 of Revenue a year at just 18% gross profit, less than half the current 40% margin. Option 2 is launching a heritage cookware range expected to add $45,000 of gross profit for $18,000 of marketing spend. The directors must decide by 30 December and want to keep dividend payments steady.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'dividend'.
questions.model_answer: A dividend is a distribution of a company's profit paid to its shareholders, usually relative to the number of shares held, from the profits of the business [2].

Usually based on the number of shares held

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why dividends matter to Fernglen Enamelware's shareholders.

scenario_stem:
Sumpter & Moss Hardware Ltd is a private limited company in Country X running two hardware stores in a market town, selling paint, tools and kitchen fittings. For the year ended 31 December 2026, the income statement showed Revenue of $410,000, Cost of Sales of $287,000, Gross Profit of $123,000, Expenses of $82,000 and Profit for the year of $41,000. A dividend of $15,000 left Retained Profit of $26,000.

Profit was earned but the bank account is overdrawn by $12,000 after the Christmas stock build-up. A supermarket-style DIY warehouse opens on the ring road in March 2027. Directors are weighing Option 1, focusing on high-margin kitchen-fitting work at 45% gross profit, against Option 2, matching warehouse prices on paint and tools, which would cut the gross profit margin from 30% towards 25%.

questions.question_text: Calculate the gross profit margin.
questions.model_answer: Gross Profit Margin = Gross Profit ÷ Revenue × 100 = $123,000 ÷ $410,000 × 100 = 30% [2].

knowledge_max_2: Correct formula: gross profit divided by revenue, times 100
Correct answer: 30%

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why understanding cost of sales matters to Sumpter & Moss Hardware.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Cost of Sales of $287,000 is 70% of Revenue, so small buying inefficiencies quickly erode the $123,000 Gross Profit and the 30% margin [k][app]. Reason 2: Knowing which lines carry the best margin, such as kitchen fittings at 45%, tells directors where to steer customers, stock investment and promotions [k][app].

knowledge_max_2: Cost of sales directly determines gross profit and margin
Margin by product line guides stock and promotion decisions
application_max_2: $287,000 Cost of Sales is 70% of $410,000 Revenue
Kitchen-fitting work at 45% gross profit vs 30% store average

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the directors should monitor the gross profit margin before the March 2027 superstore opens.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: The margin is already only 30%, so Option 2, matching warehouse prices, could drag it towards 25% [k][app], wiping out profit without volume gains to compensate [an]. Point 2: Steering towards 45%-margin kitchen-fitting work under Option 1 [k][app] would raise the blended margin and protect the $41,000 Profit for the year from erosion [an].

knowledge_max_2: A lower margin before a rival opens leaves no buffer for a price war
Shifting the sales mix towards higher-margin work protects profit
application_max_2: Option 2 could cut margin from 30% towards 25%
Kitchen-fitting work at 45% under Option 1; Profit for the year is $41,000
analysis_max_2: Competing on price against a superstore with buying power destroys profit
A richer sales mix defends profit without needing higher volumes

questions.question_text: Do you think the directors should focus on high-margin kitchen-fitting work (Option 1) or match warehouse prices on paint and tools (Option 2)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option 1 concentrates on 45% gross profit kitchen-fitting work, which should lift the blended margin above the current 30% and defend profit without fighting the warehouse on price [k][app][an]. Option 2 matches the new rival head-on, but cutting the margin from 30% towards 25% would sharply reduce Profit for the year from $41,000 unless volumes rise a great deal [k][an].
